comments.body: Every GitHub login fails when the token response has no `expires_in`. Line 110 `Date.now() + response.expires_in * 1000` (and line 113 `response.refresh_token_expires_in`) yields NaN when the field is absent. `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` throws RangeError, which the catch at lines 126-127 turns into `{ success: false, error: "Invalid time value" }`. GitHub OAuth Apps, and GitHub Apps without token expiration, return only `access_token`, `scope` and `token_type`, so the provider cannot log in with them. The test mock always returns `expires_in`, so this path is not exercised. The same happens on a bad code: GitHub returns HTTP 200 with an `error` body, so the `!r.ok` check at lines 94-100 does not fire, and the user sees the misleading "Invalid time value" instead of GitHub's error.

`upsert_` never checks that the `/user` response is OK. Lines 144-151 read `const entity_id = user.id` from whatever body comes back. When GitHub returns an error body (for example a 403 rate limit or a 5xx on a valid token), `entity_id` is undefined. `authIdentityService.update(undefined, ...)` at line 811 in the same file then builds a filter with `entity_id: undefined`. `buildWhere` in packages/core/utils/src/modules-sdk/build-query.ts (lines 101-107) passes undefined values through unchanged. Unless the ORM drops undefined where-keys, which I did not verify, the query matches every `github` provider identity. If exactly one exists, its provider metadata is overwritten with the caller's token and that existing identity is returned as authenticated, so the caller is issued a JWT for another user's account.

The GET auth-start endpoint no longer redirects. Line 50 `return res.status(200).json({ location })` replaces the previous `res.redirect(location)`. A browser navigation or `<a href="/auth/user/google">` to this route now shows the JSON body `{ "location": ... }` and never reaches the provider. The PR's breaking-change list covers the callback and the Google option renames but not this change to the start route. Clients that followed the redirect from the GET endpoint break.

The OAuth flow has no `state` parameter, so login CSRF is possible. `getRedirect` (lines 188-202) and `validateCallback` accept any `code` with no binding to the initiating session. An attacker can start the flow with their own GitHub account, obtain the `code` from the callback URL, and get a victim's browser to request `/auth/user/github/callback?code=...`. The victim's app then stores a token for the attacker's identity. The TODO acknowledges the gap, but this provider is new in this change and ships without the protection.
